passage: The notice board in the nursing college hostel in Mangaluru had a new sheet pinned beside the mess timings: Sangeeta's chart. Two columns, "Lights out by 11" and "Two hours of study before dinner", with a tick or a cross for every day of September. In August she'd been sleeping at two, dozing through anatomy, and blaming the hostel noise. Now the chart showed twenty-two ticks in the first column and nineteen in the second. Her roommate Gopika stopped to read it on the way to breakfast. "You put it where everyone can see?" "That's the point," Sangeeta said. "If I cross it, it's me who crossed it." That week her anatomy quiz mark jumped from eleven to seventeen. She drew a small star next to it and stood a little straighter at assembly.

qa.q: How many ticks did the chart show in the first column?
qa.a: The chart showed twenty-two ticks in the first column.

qa.q: What does 'If I cross it, it's me who crossed it' show about Sangeeta's thinking?
qa.a: She now sees herself as responsible for her results instead of the hostel noise, and that ownership feels motivating rather than heavy 🙂

qa.q: What choice made Sangeeta's progress visible, and why did that matter?
qa.a: Pinning the chart on the notice board and marking the quiz score beside it; the ticks and the jump from eleven to seventeen gave her proof that her own changes worked.

qa.q: How might Gopika see the chart on the notice board?
qa.a: Gopika seems surprised that Sangeeta would make it public, and may be impressed, perhaps even tempted to try a chart of Gopika's own.

grounding: A student fixes her sleep and study schedule, records it publicly and gains confidence from seeing results she caused.

passage:
Dear Binita,
You asked in your last letter whether I'm still "the zombie of Room 12". Not anymore, I think. In January I decided to change two things myself: sleep by midnight, and study from seven to nine every evening in the reading room, not in bed. I drew a small table in my diary and filled it in every night. The first two weeks were ugly, five crosses. But by March the table was mostly ticks, and something odd happened. My mid-sem marks went up in three subjects out of four. The fourth, economics, stayed the same, so I know it isn't magic. Still, looking at those ticks, I feel as if I wrote them. Not luck, not my roommate being quiet. Me.
Write soon,
Tenzin

qa.q: What two things did Tenzin decide to change in January?
qa.a: Sleep by midnight, and study from seven to nine every evening in the reading room.

qa.q: How does Tenzin feel looking at the ticks, and why?
qa.a: Proud and more confident; the ticks and the higher marks feel like proof that Tenzin, not luck or a quiet roommate, made the change.

qa.q: What choice kept Tenzin going through the ugly first weeks?
qa.a: Filling in the diary table every night, crosses included; the record made progress visible, so by March the ticks could show what had really changed.

qa.q: How might Binita read this letter, having known 'the zombie of Room 12'?
qa.a: Binita would likely be amused and pleased, noticing Tenzin sounds surer, and honest enough to admit that economics didn't move.

grounding: A student changes sleep and study habits, records them, and feels like the author of the improved results.

subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]
passage: Rafael came home from school in Seville and threw his maths test on the kitchen table. Four out of ten. "Señora Ortiz hates me," he said. "She was in a bad mood, so she marked hard." His older brother Javier, sixteen, picked up the paper. "Did you practise the fractions she gave you?" "What's the point? Last time I got six and I didn't practise either. It's luck." "Lucía got ten." "Because she sits at the front. Teachers like the front." Javier turned the page over. Every wrong answer was a fraction sum from the practice sheet, still folded in Rafael's bag, blank. Rafael didn't look. He was already switching on the TV, sure that next week would depend on Señora Ortiz's mood too.

qa.q: What mark did Rafael get on the maths test?
qa.a: Four out of ten.

qa.q: Why does blaming Señora Ortiz's mood feel right to Rafael?
qa.a: It spares him the idea that practice matters; if marks are luck or mood, a low score isn't his fault and skipping the sheet costs nothing.

qa.q: What could Javier try to help Rafael see the link between preparation and marks?
qa.a: Sit with him to do the blank practice sheet, point out that the wrong answers were exactly those sums, and compare next week's result.

qa.q: What might Javier be thinking as he turns the page over?
qa.a: Javier probably sees the pattern clearly, wrong answers matching the blank sheet, and may feel frustrated that his younger brother won't look.

grounding: A child blames the teacher's mood and luck for low marks and never connects them with his skipped practice.

subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]
passage: At the government school in Indore, the weekly spelling test came back on Friday. Gautam, nine, had six out of twenty. He shoved the paper into his desk. "Nikita Ma'am gives me the hardest words," he told his bench-mate. "She reads fast when it's my row." Nikita Ma'am, walking past, heard. She crouched beside him. "Gautam, which words did you practise this week?" He shrugged. "None. It doesn't matter. Some weeks I'm lucky, some weeks not." "Last month you practised with your sister and got fourteen, remember?" Gautam frowned. "That was a good day." He picked at the edge of the desk. It had not occurred to him that the good day and the practice might be the same thing.

qa.q: What did Gautam score on the spelling test?
qa.a: Six out of twenty.

qa.q: Why does Gautam call the fourteen 'a good day'?
qa.a: He believes results come from luck or Ma'am's speed, so even his best score seems like chance rather than something his practice caused.

qa.q: What could Nikita Ma'am do next to help Gautam link practice and marks?
qa.a: Start a simple weekly chart of words practised and marks, so Gautam can see the practice and the fourteen side by side.

qa.q: How might Nikita Ma'am feel hearing that she reads fast for his row?
qa.a: She may feel a little stung but more concerned, seeing that Gautam believes his marks depend on her rather than on his preparation.

grounding: A child says the teacher gives him hard words and that marks are luck, never linking results with practice.

passage:
Thursday night
Farhan got suspended for a week for bunking the maths exam. On Tuesday he'd asked me to tell Ma'am he was sick, and I said no. So it's my fault. If I'd covered for him he wouldn't be in trouble, and his Ammi wouldn't have cried at the school gate. I couldn't eat dinner.
Told Amma at bedtime. I thought she'd say, "Yes, you should have helped." Instead she put her phone down and hugged me. She said, "Ganga, you didn't choose to skip the exam. Farhan did. Saying no to lying was right." She said I can still be a good friend: message him, share my notes.
I still feel heavy. But lighter than at dinner.
Sending him the notes tomorrow.

qa.q: Why was Farhan suspended?
qa.a: Farhan got suspended for a week for bunking the maths exam.

qa.q: Why does Ganga feel it's all Ganga's fault?
qa.a: Because Ganga refused to cover for Farhan, that 'no' seems to have caused the suspension and his Ammi's tears; taking on that much control turns into guilt.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Ganga decide after it?
qa.a: Amma saying that Farhan chose to skip and that refusing to lie was right; Ganga decided to stay a good friend by sending the notes instead of carrying the blame.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when Ganga's notes arrive?
qa.a: Farhan might feel relieved that his friend isn't angry or distant, and supported while catching up on a week of missed classes.

grounding: A teenager blames themselves for a friend's choice to skip an exam until a parent helps separate responsibility.

subtype: Balanced view of luck and effort [Response]
passage:
Dear Jomon,
You asked how I feel about not getting into the architecture college in Thiruvananthapuram. Honestly, both things are true. I didn't practise enough freehand drawing; I know that. I spent too long on maths I already knew. But I also got the year when the paper had three perspective questions instead of one, and my exam centre had a power cut for twenty minutes. That was luck, and it wasn't mine.
So I'm not calling myself stupid, and I'm not blaming the universe. I've joined a weekend drawing class, and I'm making a timetable that puts drawing first. If the paper's cruel again next year, fine. At least the drawing part will be mine.
Your sister,
Seema

qa.q: How long was the power cut at Seema's exam centre?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How does Seema feel about the result, and what shows it isn't just blame?
qa.a: Disappointed but steady; Seema admits not practising enough freehand drawing and also names the harder paper and the power cut, refusing both 'stupid' and 'the universe'.

qa.q: What choices does Seema make about the parts she can influence?
qa.a: Joining a weekend drawing class and making a timetable that puts drawing first, while accepting that next year's paper may be hard again.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel reading this letter from Seema?
qa.a: Jomon would probably be relieved that Seema isn't crushed or bitter, and might take a lesson about handling setbacks too.

grounding: A student sees that both her own preparation and bad luck shaped an admission result, and acts on the part she can change.

subtype: Balanced view of luck and effort [Response]
passage: Himani, you keep saying I'm lucky I got into the Delhi college. Okay, let me be honest. Yes, I was lucky. My school had a proper library and a teacher who stayed after class for us. My parents could pay for entrance coaching; lots of families can't. And the economics paper that year was easy. All luck. But I also woke up at five for eight months and did every past paper twice. Both things happened. I try to remember both, because if I only remember the luck, I feel like a fraud, and if I only remember the work, I start judging people who didn't get in. So this semester I just work on what I can: attendance, notes, sleep. The rest I let go. I'm Sarita, by the way, not a genius.

qa.q: What did Sarita do for eight months?
qa.a: Sarita woke up at five and did every past paper twice.

qa.q: Why does Sarita try to remember both luck and effort?
qa.a: Remembering only luck makes Sarita feel like a fraud, and only effort leads to judging others; holding both keeps the pride honest and the view of others kind.

qa.q: What does Sarita focus on this semester, and why is that wise?
qa.a: Attendance, notes and sleep, the parts within reach; acting on those while letting go of the rest avoids both blame and helplessness.

qa.q: How might Himani hear Sarita's answer to 'you're lucky'?
qa.a: Himani might feel taken seriously rather than brushed off, since Sarita agrees about the luck while also sharing the hidden work.

grounding: A student recognises that luck and effort both shaped an admission and focuses on the parts within reach.

passage:
Dear Yusuf,
You asked what my father meant when he said "it's all in the stars" at the wedding. I've been thinking about it since. Papa checks the almanac before every big step and says whatever is written will happen. I used to think that meant he left things to fate. Then I watched him this year. When the shop's permit was delayed, he said, "Karma will sort it," and then went to the municipal office four times, with every paper copied twice. When I asked how those fit together, he laughed. "God decides the harvest. I still plough the field." I think I understand now. He trusts something bigger, and it seems to make him calmer, not lazier.
Love,
Reena

qa.q: How many times did Papa go to the municipal office?
qa.a: He went to the municipal office four times.

qa.q: Why did Reena's view of Papa's belief change?
qa.a: Watching him chase the permit with every paper copied twice showed Reena that trusting fate didn't make him passive; if anything it seemed to calm him.

qa.q: What choice did Papa make when the permit was delayed, and what does it show?
qa.a: He said karma would sort it and still went to the office four times with copies; trust in larger forces and doing his own part went together.

qa.q: How might Yusuf understand Papa's words after reading the letter?
qa.a: Yusuf might see 'it's all in the stars' not as giving up but as a way to stay calm while still working hard.

grounding: A young person notices that their father trusts fate and karma while still working hard, and sees the two need not clash.

passage: Madhav, you laughed when my Ajji said the new tiffin contract was "up to Chamundeshwari". I laughed too, once. But I stayed with her in Mysuru for three weeks this summer, and I watched. Every morning she lit the lamp and said, "Whatever is meant will come." Then she was at the stove by five, tasting every dal, checking every box before the delivery boy left. When the college canteen tender came up, she prayed, and she also made me type her menu three times until the prices were exactly right. She got it. When I asked whether it was the goddess or the menu, she tapped my head. "Why do you think it has to be one?" I'm Darshan, and I'm starting to think her faith just meant she didn't panic while she worked.

qa.q: What did Ajji make Darshan do with her menu?
qa.a: She made Darshan type her menu three times until the prices were exactly right.

qa.q: What does Ajji's tap on the head suggest she thinks of Darshan's question?
qa.a: She seems amused and sure; for her, trusting the goddess and doing the work belong together, so choosing one seems a silly split.

qa.q: What in Ajji's approach could Darshan use in daily work?
qa.a: Keeping a belief that brings calm while still doing the careful parts, like checking every box, so faith steadies the effort instead of replacing it.

qa.q: How might Madhav see Ajji differently after hearing this?
qa.a: Madhav might stop seeing her words as passive and notice discipline and trust working side by side.

grounding: A young adult watches a grandmother trust in the goddess while working carefully and sees that faith and effort can coexist.

passage:
Dear Madhav,
Thanks for asking about the shop. Short answer: it's closed. Not my fault, honestly. First the landlord raised the rent. Then the online sellers started undercutting everything. Then the monsoon flooded the lane in July, and nobody walks down a lane full of water. It's the same story as the printing job in 2022: a boss who never liked me, a market that went bad. Some people are just born unlucky, and I'm one of them.
You asked in your last email whether I'd ever gone through the numbers with an accountant, or asked customers why they stopped coming. I don't see the point. You can't argue with luck.
Anyway, I'm looking at a new franchise. Different area. Should be better.
Darshan

qa.q: What flooded the lane in July?
qa.a: The monsoon flooded the lane in July.

qa.q: Why might Darshan prefer to blame the landlord, the market and luck?
qa.a: If every setback comes from outside, Darshan's pride stays intact; going through the numbers might reveal a share that would hurt to see.

qa.q: What went wrong in Darshan's thinking, and what small step could help before the franchise?
qa.a: Darshan never looks at any personal part in the closures; going through the old shop's numbers with an accountant and asking a few former customers could show what to change.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel reading 'I don't see the point'?
qa.a: Madhav may feel shut out and worried, having offered a way to learn from the closure, and fear the same story will repeat with the franchise.

grounding: An adult blames the landlord, the market and luck for repeated failures and refuses to examine any personal part.

passage: Siddharth, you want to know why I left the bank? I'll tell you straight. The branch manager had favourites, and I wasn't one of them. Three years, three bad appraisals. First year it was the targets, which nobody could meet in that area. Second year, a new manager who didn't know me. Third year, bad luck, the audit landed in my month. I'm Manoj, I'm good at what I do, and the system just didn't see it. You're asking whether the feedback ever said the same thing? Well... they said my loan-file paperwork was always late. All three years. But that's the kind of thing managers write when they've already decided. Anyway, the next job will be different. It always starts well.

qa.q: How many bad appraisals did Manoj get?
qa.a: Three years, three bad appraisals.

qa.q: What does Manoj's pause at 'Well...' suggest?
qa.a: A flicker of discomfort; the same feedback three years running hints at a pattern Manoj would rather not face, so it gets explained away to protect pride.

qa.q: What could Manoj do before the next job to break the pattern?
qa.a: Take the repeated note about late loan-file paperwork seriously and set up a simple way to track and finish each file on time, instead of blaming each manager.

qa.q: What might Siddharth be thinking when asking about the feedback?
qa.a: Siddharth seems to suspect a common thread and tests it gently, perhaps hoping Manoj will see a personal share before the next job.

grounding: An adult blames managers and luck for repeated bad appraisals and brushes aside the one piece of feedback that keeps recurring.

passage: Dhruv, your Nani tells me you won't touch the puzzle book I sent, only the easy colouring one. Come, sit with your old Manoj Nana. When I was nine, everyone in our house called me "the clever one". "Manoj is so smart," at every wedding, every festival. I loved it. But here's the funny thing: I started running from hard sums. If the teacher put a tricky question on the board, I pretended not to see it. If I got it wrong, they'd find out I wasn't clever after all. My cousin, whom nobody called clever, tried everything and got stuck all the time, and by twelve he was better at maths than me. Being "the clever one" felt like carrying a glass bowl. I was so scared of dropping it that I stopped walking.

qa.q: What did everyone in the house call young Manoj?
qa.a: 'The clever one.'

qa.q: Why did young Manoj pretend not to see tricky questions?
qa.a: He feared a wrong answer would prove he wasn't clever after all; protecting the label made trying feel dangerous.

qa.q: What could the family have praised instead, and how might that have changed things?
qa.a: His trying and his methods rather than his cleverness; then getting stuck wouldn't threaten who he was, and hard sums would feel safe to attempt.

qa.q: What might Dhruv realise about the puzzle book after this story?
qa.a: Dhruv might see that avoiding the puzzle book protects a label, and that trying and getting stuck, as the cousin did, is how people get better.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how being called clever as a child made him avoid hard problems to protect the label.

passage: The inter-school quiz in Bhopal started late because a bus broke down, so each team had only two minutes to choose a round: "Easy Picks", or the "Challenge Round" for double points. Jeevan, ten, had heard "You're our little genius" from his mother, Rashmi, every day since he could read. She'd said it again that morning at the gate. His teammates wanted the Challenge Round. Jeevan's stomach clenched. What if he got one wrong, up on the stage, with Mummy in the second row? "Easy Picks," he insisted, so firmly that the others gave in. They won the easy round easily. On the bus home, Rashmi said, "My genius!" Jeevan stared out of the window and didn't answer. He wasn't sure why he felt worse, not better.

qa.q: Why did each team have only two minutes to choose a round?
qa.a: The inter-school quiz started late because a bus broke down.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan's stomach clench at the idea of the Challenge Round?
qa.a: He feared getting one wrong on stage in front of his mother and losing the 'genius' label 😰, so the harder round felt dangerous.

qa.q: What could Rashmi say on the bus to make challenge feel safer next time?
qa.a: Praise the effort and teamwork, and say she'd be proud of him for trying the harder round even if they got some wrong.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's teammates see his insistence on Easy Picks?
qa.a: They wanted the Challenge Round and might feel let down or puzzled, not knowing that the 'genius' label made him afraid of a single mistake.

grounding: A child constantly called a genius avoids the harder quiz round to keep the label, and the praise leaves him uneasy.

passage: In the Class 3 room of a Hyderabad school, Aparna had been stuck on the same puzzle for ten minutes: move matchsticks to make three triangles out of nine sticks. First she laid them in a row. Then she tried a star. Then she drew it on paper, rubbed it out, and tried again, tongue between her teeth. Finally the three triangles clicked. Rukmini Ma'am came over. "Aparna, I watched you. You tried a row, then a star, then you drew it out. When one way didn't work, you changed the way. That's why you got it." Aparna looked at her matchsticks, then up. "Can I try the harder one? The four triangles?" Rukmini Ma'am smiled and handed her the card.

qa.q: How many matchsticks did Aparna have to work with?
qa.a: Nine sticks.

qa.q: Why does Aparna ask for the harder puzzle right away?
qa.a: Hearing that changing her approach is what worked made her feel she could do it again, so a harder puzzle seemed exciting rather than risky.

qa.q: Which part of Rukmini Ma'am's praise mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Naming the exact steps, row, star, drawing, and the switch between them; it tells Aparna that her methods and persistence, not luck, solved the puzzle.

qa.q: How might a classmate who gave up early feel hearing Rukmini Ma'am's words?
qa.a: That classmate might realise that getting stuck is normal and that trying different ways is what worked, and feel encouraged to try again.

grounding: A teacher praises a child for changing methods until one worked, and the child immediately seeks a harder challenge.

passage:
"Mausi, I got it! The kite-string sum!"
Ishita Mausi put down her tea. "The one you called impossible at lunch?"
"Yes! First I tried adding, wrong. Then I drew the kite and the string, still wrong. Then I made a table like you do on your board."
"Show me." Mausi read the page slowly. "Aditi, look at what you did. You didn't stop when adding failed. You drew it. When the drawing didn't work, you changed again. The table worked because you'd already ruled out two ways."

qa.q: What choice does Ishita Mausi make in her answer, and why does it help?
qa.a: She describes each method and says ability grows by changing approaches; that makes Aditi want the tough problem instead of protecting a label.

qa.q: How might Ishita Mausi feel when Aditi asks for the tough one?
qa.a: Ishita Mausi is probably delighted 😊, seeing that praise for the process has made a challenge feel inviting rather than scary.

grounding: An aunt who is a teacher praises a child's switching of methods, teaching that ability grows, and the child asks for a harder problem.

passage: Last year I quit the drawing club after two weeks, and I told everyone the same thing: "I'm just not a creative person." I'm Yusuf. Our first exercise was drawing a hand, and mine looked like a bunch of bananas. Abhinav, next to me, drew one that looked real, with wrinkles on the knuckles. I remember thinking, some people have it and some don't, so why waste Saturdays? It felt like a fact, like being tall. This summer Abhinav showed me his old sketchbook from Class 6. His hands looked like bananas too. Worse than mine, honestly. He'd just kept going for three years. I haven't gone back to the club yet. But I've stopped saying "I'm not creative." Now I say, "I'm not good at hands yet."

qa.q: What did Yusuf's first drawing of a hand look like?
qa.a: It looked like a bunch of bananas.

qa.q: Why did quitting feel sensible to Yusuf at the time?
qa.a: Next to Abhinav's real-looking hand, talent seemed fixed, 'like being tall', so more Saturdays seemed a waste for someone who didn't have it.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yusuf, and what did it change?
qa.a: Seeing Abhinav's Class 6 sketchbook full of banana hands; Yusuf stopped saying 'I'm not creative' and started saying 'not good at hands yet'.

qa.q: Why might Abhinav have shown Yusuf the old sketchbook?
qa.a: Abhinav may have noticed Yusuf giving up and wanted to show that his own skill came from three years of practice, not a gift.

grounding: A teenager who drew poorly decided to be 'just not creative' and quit, turning a current level into a permanent limit.

passage:
Art teacher's note, Class 9, 8 February. Irawati.
Sarika has stopped handing in drawings. When I asked, she said, "I'm just not creative, Ma'am. Some people are born artists. I'm not." Her first portrait this term was stiff, and she compared it with Rinchen's, which is very good. Since then she has handed in blank sheets with only her name on them. What worries me is that she's turning where she is now into where she'll always be. Today I showed her three of my own drawings from college, clumsy ones, and asked for one ten-minute sketch of her shoe, nothing else. She did it, grumbling. The laces were good, and I told her exactly what was good about them. Next week: the shoe again, from a different angle.

qa.q: What has Sarika handed in since the first portrait?
qa.a: Blank sheets with only her name on them.

qa.q: What does Sarika believe about talent when she says 'Some people are born artists'?
qa.a: She believes talent is fixed, so her stiff first portrait feels like a permanent verdict and trying again seems pointless.

qa.q: What choice did Irawati make today, and why might it help?
qa.a: Showing her own clumsy college drawings and asking for one ten-minute shoe sketch; a small task plus specific praise for the laces shows that skill can grow.

qa.q: What worries Irawati most about Sarika's words?
qa.a: Irawati worries that Sarika is turning her current level into a lifelong limit, and seems to care more about that belief than about any one missing drawing.

grounding: An art teacher sees a teenager decide she is just not creative and stop, and responds with a small task and specific praise.

Keerthana got the solo in the college dance showcase. Again. Everyone crowded around her in the green room, and I clapped too, but my face felt stiff.

qa.a: Keerthana might sense distance from a friend she started with and feel confused or a little hurt, not knowing it comes from Ayesha feeling threatened.

qa.q: What does 'every time his name comes up I feel sick' reveal?
qa.a: Kalyani feels threatened rather than inspired; with talent seen as fixed, Mehul's success feels like proof of Kalyani's own permanent limit.

qa.q: What could Kalyani try instead of avoiding the topic?
qa.a: Look at how Mehul practised since Class 8 and set a small weekly practice goal, treating the 200-point gap as years of work rather than a gift.

qa.q: How does Ritu see Mehul's lead differently from Kalyani?

grounding: A student decides a peer's lead is inborn and feels threatened, while a friend points to years of practice.
